chunks: And as for what Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar from Bakr ibn Salih, who said:

I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'My son is with me, and I have ordered him to perform Hajj on behalf of my mother. Will one Hajj suffice for her?' He wrote back: 'No.' And his son was a 'sarrurah' (one who performs Hajj for others) and his mother was a 'sarrarah' (one for whom Hajj is performed). The meaning in this report is that we interpret it as the son having wealth, so it was not permissible for him to perform Hajj on behalf of his mother until he had performed Hajj for himself, or he gave [the cost of] a 'sarrurah' who had no wealth, according to what we have previously established, and this interpretation does not contradict [the other reports].

key_terms.التَّأْوِيل: Interpretation or understanding of the legal ruling
key_terms.حَجَّة الْإِسْلَام: The first obligatory Hajj performed by a Muslim
key_terms.صَرُورَة: A person who performs Hajj on behalf of others, often for a fee
key_terms.لَا مَالَ لَهُ: Having no wealth (referring to the poor person hired for Hajj)

ai.seo_question: Can a son perform Hajj for his mother if he has not yet performed his own obligatory Hajj?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Jawad clarifies the priority of the obligatory Hajj (*Hajjat al-Islam*) over performing Hajj on behalf of others, resolving a query from Bakr ibn Salih. The Imam’s ruling that a son with wealth must first fulfill his own duty or delegate to a poor person (*sarrarah*) highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that personal obligations take precedence before vicarious acts. This establishes a clear hierarchy in Hajj performance, ensuring the individual’s spiritual debt is settled before assuming responsibility for another.
